newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN ZULU PARTY SEEKS VETERAN PENSIONS.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN ZULU PARTY SEEKS VETERAN PENSIONS.

text.p: South Africa's ruling African National Congress (ANC) on Tuesday turned down a request by the rival Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) to be included in a pension scheme for veterans of the struggle against apartheid.

IFP legislator Gavin Woods said on Tuesday that veteran allies of conservative Zulu Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi's fight against white rule should be treated in the same way as veterans of President Nelson Mandela's party.
The ANC and the IFP have been locked in a bitter political turf war in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province since the ANC was legalised in 1990.
The IFP walked out of final constitutional talks in Cape Town on Monday because the ANC had refused to accede to its request for virtual autonomy in IFP-ruled KwaZulu-Natal province.
Woods told parliament's powerful finance committee that definitions in the Special Pensions Bill before parliament should be changed to include the IFP.

At present the bill proposes modest pensions of up to 42,000 rand ($9,275) a year for former permanent employees of outlawed political movements such as the ANC, the Pan Africanist Congress and the South African Communist Party.
"The IFP is concerned about fairness. It is a very topical issue within the party," Woods told the multiparty committee.
He said that though the IFP was never banned, its members suffered more than ANC members because it not have the foreign support given to the ANC in exile.
ANC member Barbara Hogan said Mandela's party, which dominates the committee, would oppose the IFP's request for inclusion "with regret".

She said the draft law would give pension rights to permanent staff of the ANC and other organisations forced into exile because the banning of their groups had made it impossible for them to accumulate pension rights.

"This is not a struggle pension, much as we wish it was. It is a compensation for people who were marginalised under apartheid and prevented from earning a pension," she told reporters after the meeting.
Woods told reporters after the ANC had denied his request that the IFP would oppose the bill when parliament votes on it later this year.

"Part of the animosity between ourselves and the ANC has been because they refuse to recognise the IFP as a bona fide liberation movement, which made a significant contribution to the fight against apartheid," he said.
The bill provides for pensions of between 6,000 rand and 42,000 rand a year for people who were in the permanent employ of a banned organisation for at least five years.
Hogan said the government estimated that up to 22,000 people might qualify for a pension, which would be payable from the age of 60.
The bill also provides for payments equivalent to two years of pension to survivors of people who died in prison or were assassinated and for payments to people maimed in the struggle.
Hogan said any attempt to extend the special pension scheme to people who fought apartheid legally would cost the country far too much.
